title: Consider exposing a stable native API for S7 interoperability
description:
I'm using S7 objects from Rust via [savvy](https://github.com/yutannihilation/savvy) in https://github.com/pola-rs/r-polars.

The upcoming S7 1.0.0 changes how class definitions are stored internally (#742), which highlighted that native extensions currently need to rely on implementation details or call back into R.

Would it make sense to expose a small, stable native API through `R_RegisterCCallable()` / `R_GetCCallable()`?

Two potentially useful operations are:

- Retrieve an S7 class definition from an instance, independent of its internal representation.
- Retrieve an S7 property, respecting custom getters rather than accessing attributes directly.

S7 already implements these operations in C (`S7_class_()` and `prop_()`), so exposing suitable wrappers might require relatively little additional code.

This would enable interoperability with Rust bindings such as savvy, as well as C/C++ extensions, without depending on S7 internals.

title: `str.S7_object()` output is affected by recent R-devel `str()` change
description:
A recent R-devel change removed the leading space from `str()` output.

S7's `str_nest()` appears to rely on this space, resulting in inconsistent output between R-release and R-devel:

```diff
- @ x: logi TRUE
+ @ x:logi TRUE
```

This is causing snapshot test failures in r-polars (https://github.com/pola-rs/r-polars/actions/runs/41486813749).

Would it make sense for S7 to handle the spacing explicitly rather than relying on `str()`?

title: Reverse-dependency updates for the next S7 release
description: This tracks downstream updates identified during reverse-dependency checks against development S7. The PRs are grouped by the changes they contain; packages can appear in several categories. [Jump to downstream PR status](#user-content-s7-downstream-pr-status) ### Avoid conflicting `:=` imports S7 now exports `:=`. Packages importing it from both S7 and rlang or data.table get an import-replacement warning. These patches retain S7’s operator and exclude the rlang or data.table placeholder. For example: ```r #' @import S7 #' @import rlang, except = ":=" NULL ``` The same applies to data.table. Existing uses of `:=` inside tidy evaluation or data.table expressions continue to work. **PRs:** [ale](https://github.com/tripartio/ale/pull/45), [apa7](https://github.com/wjschne/apa7/pull/2), [ellmer](https://github.com/tidyverse/ellmer/pull/1181), [GGally](https://github.com/ggobi/ggally/pull/578), [joinery](https://github.com/edubruell/joinery/pull/1), [rtemis](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis/pull/206), [rtemis.a3](https://github.com/rtemis-org/a3/pull/20), [rtemis.core](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis.core/pull/28), [rtemis.llm](https://github.com/rtemis-org/llm/pull/19), [shinyOAuth](https://github.com/lukakoning/shinyOAuth/pull/23). ### Use S7’s package lifecycle hooks The patches adopt the current package hooks: - `S7_on_load()` registers methods when the package loads. - `S7_on_build()` removes temporary bindings left by method registration, so calls to imported generics still find the original functions. It runs at the top level, after method declarations. - `S7_on_unload()` cleans up S7 method registrations and dependency hooks when the package unloads. The build hook directly fixes failures in packages such as btw, filtro, mighty.metadata, and mixtime, where imported functions were left bound to registration placeholders. Other packages receive the lifecycle updates alongside their compatibility fixes; each hook addition does not represent a separate revdep failure. Packages retaining support for older S7 guard the new hooks and keep `methods_register()` as the load fallback. **PRs:** [ale](https://github.com/tripartio/ale/pull/45), [apa7](https://github.com/wjschne/apa7/pull/2), [bidsr](https://github.com/dipterix/bidsr/pull/1), [btw](https://github.com/posit-dev/btw/pull/240), [GGally](https://github.com/ggobi/ggally/pull/578), [ggarrow](https://github.com/teunbrand/ggarrow/pull/20), [ggdiagram](https://github.com/wjschne/ggdiagram/pull/9), [gglogger](https://github.com/pwwang/gglogger/pull/2), [ggpath](https://github.com/mrcaseb/ggpath/pull/25), [ggplot2](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/6914), [GitAI](https://github.com/r-world-devs/GitAI/pull/118), [imply](https://github.com/jonclayden/imply/pull/1), [joinery](https://github.com/edubruell/joinery/pull/1), [marquee](https://github.com/r-lib/marquee/pull/107), [medfit](https://github.com/Data-Wise/medfit/pull/214), [mighty.metadata](https://github.com/NovoNordisk-OpenSource/mighty.metadata/pull/73), [mixtime](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/mixtime/pull/105), [myTAI](https://github.com/drostlab/myTAI/pull/80), [nflplotR](https://github.com/nflverse/nflplotR/pull/98), [rtemis](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis/pull/206), [rtemis.a3](https://github.com/rtemis-org/a3/pull/20), [rtemis.core](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis.core/pull/28), [shinychat](https://github.com/posit-dev/shinychat/pull/429), [shinyfilters](https://github.com/joshwlivingston/shinyfilters/pull/153), [shinyOAuth](https://github.com/lukakoning/shinyOAuth/pull/23), [statim](https://github.com/s7-stats/statim/pull/27), [vecvec](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/vecvec/pull/30). ### Update constructors and inherited properties Several custom constructors pass a class definition or an unrelated `S7_object()` as their parent. These patches construct an instance of the declared parent instead. Other changes pass the parent positionally to accommodate the renamed `new_object()` argument, or name arguments when forwarding them through generated constructors. **PRs:** [bidsr](https://github.com/dipterix/bidsr/pull/1), [btw](https://github.com/posit-dev/btw/pull/240), [caugi](https://github.com/frederikfabriciusbjerre/caugi/pull/344), [cohortBuilder](https://github.com/r-world-devs/cohortBuilder/pull/89), [deltapif](https://github.com/RodrigoZepeda/deltapif/pull/2), [ggarrow](https://github.com/teunbrand/ggarrow/pull/20), [ggdiagram](https://github.com/wjschne/ggdiagram/pull/9), [ggpath](https://github.com/mrcaseb/ggpath/pull/25), [mighty.metadata](https://github.com/NovoNordisk-OpenSource/mighty.metadata/pull/73), [rtemis.a3](https://github.com/rtemis-org/a3/pull/20), [S7schema](https://github.com/NovoNordisk-OpenSource/S7schema/pull/80). Related property changes: - [dcmstan](https://github.com/r-dcm/dcmstan/pull/23) uses getter-only inherited properties and generated constructors. The parent initializes and validates the model identifier; the child makes it read-only afterward. - [ggpath](https://github.com/mrcaseb/ggpath/pull/25) stores image dimensions in `image_size`, avoiding a conflict with the inherited numeric `size` property. - [rtemis](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis/pull/206) preserves the parent’s declared property type when reconstructing inherited runtime properties from a schema. ### Quote complex property defaults S7 now warns about complex values supplied directly as property defaults. These patches supply the expression that constructs the value, for example: ```r default <- quote(c(0, 1)) ``` This keeps the expression in the generated constructor and evaluates it for each new object. Plain scalars and empty vectors without attributes can still be supplied directly. Property factories in bidsr and rtemis also need to preserve the quoted expression while using its evaluated value for validation or metadata. **PRs:** [bidsr](https://github.com/dipterix/bidsr/pull/1), [ellmer](https://github.com/tidyverse/ellmer/pull/1181), [filtro](https://github.com/tidymodels/filtro/pull/183), [mixtime](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/mixtime/pull/105), [rtemis](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis/pull/206), [rtemis.core](https://github.com/rtemis-org/rtemis.core/pull/28), [rtemis.draw](https://github.com/rtemis-org/draw/pull/21), [shinyOAuth](https://github.com/lukakoning/shinyOAuth/pull/23). ### Other compatibility changes | Change | Packages and PRs | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Check whether an object is S7 explicitly. `S7_class()` now describes ordinary R objects too, so a non-`NULL` result no longer identifies an S7 object. | [shinyfilters](https://github.com/joshwlivingston/shinyfilters/pull/153), [statim](https://github.com/s7-stats/statim/pull/27) | | Capture the original operand expression under updated method dispatch, preserving useful error messages and replayable logs. | [ggplot2](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/6914), [gglogger](https://github.com/pwwang/gglogger/pull/2) | | Use public method discovery and lookup APIs. Store calendar membership on unit instances and preserve it through reconstruction; the arithmetic graph algorithms remain unchanged. | [mixtime](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/mixtime/pull/105) | | Match the dispatch dimensions of base `[[` and `$` generics. | [bidsr](https://github.com/dipterix/bidsr/pull/1) | | Register property unions with S4 before registering the classes that use them. | [imply](https://github.com/jonclayden/imply/pull/1), [medfit](https://github.com/Data-Wise/medfit/pull/214); [PFIM patch](https://github.com/cran/PFIM/compare/master...t-kalinowski:fix/s7-compatibility) (submission pending) | | Handle shared S7 class definitions in coverage instrumentation and serialization. | [covr](https://github.com/r-lib/covr/pull/646), [typedjson](https://github.com/nbenn/typedjson/pull/120) | | Use `S7_data()` to extract underlying image data, and update a test that assumed it removed the parent S3 class. | [imply](https://github.com/jonclayden/imply/pull/1), [ggplot2](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/pull/6914) | | Match constructor documentation to generated arguments and defaults. | [ellmer](https://github.com/tidyverse/ellmer/pull/1181), [myTAI](https://github.com/drostlab/myTAI/pull/80), [nflplotR](https://github.com/nflverse/nflplotR/pull/98), [shinychat](https://github.com/posit-dev/shinychat/pull/429) | | Preserve array dimensions during replacement and resolve callbacks in the correct evaluation context. | [vecvec](https://github.com/mitchelloharawild/vecvec/pull/30) | | Supply model configuration in mocked chat fixtures. | [GitAI](https://github.com/r-world-devs/GitAI/pull/118) | | Add a missing S7 namespace import. | [marquee](https://github.com/r-lib/marquee/pull/107) | ### Existing upstream work and submission order [measr PR #90](https://github.com/r-dcm/measr/pull/90) already covers its constructor documentation and lifecycle updates, so no separate PR is planned. The dcmstan patch builds on its maintainer’s merged S7 updates. Some patches depend on others: ggpath precedes nflplotR, S7schema precedes mighty.metadata, and rtemis.core precedes its dependents. The [PFIM patch](https://github.com/cran/PFIM/compare/master...t-kalinowski:fix/s7-compatibility) is available as a diff against the read-only `cran/PFIM` mirror. title: bug: `deparse(conditionCall(cnd))` fails for errors raised in S7 methods
description:
Errors raised inside an S7 method record a call that contains the dispatched S7 object. 
On R 4.3.3 that call can't be deparsed, so any tool using conditionCall() crashes.
```r
library(S7)

Foo <- new_class("Foo")
g <- new_generic("g", "x")
method(g, Foo) <- function(x) stop("boom")

cnd <- tryCatch(g(Foo()), error = identity)
deparse(conditionCall(cnd))
#> Error in deparse(conditionCall(cnd)) :
#>   'S4SXP': should not happen - please report
```
`rlang::as_label(conditionCall(cnd))` fails the same way.
The call's head is the `method(g, Foo)` symbol. Its dispatch argument is a forced promise holding the S7 object it looks like
[`R-devel has a commit`](https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/commit/68c0c592ce13c47bf10bd86202f9f76bd39e4b7d)  makes `deparse()` handle these objects, but released R versions still fail. 

Could S7 record a call that succesfully deparses, without expecting updating to R-devel?

title: How to modularly subclass S7 objects?
description:
Hello S7 devs,

I have originally created #566 but I did not provide a motivating example for this pattern. Specifically, in S7, If two subclasses do not interfere with each other, how can they extend the same root object at the same time? 

Suppose for example, 2 packages both extend `ggplot2::ggplot`, but neither property that they contribute interferes with the other package. This would theoretically allow both packages to build their subclass from the other. However considering how the S7_class attribute is added to the object, this enforces a fairly strict inheritance pattern in that if class C builds itself from class B, it will loose all properties from the B class.

```r
library(ggplot2)
gg <- ggplot()
class(gg)
# [1] "ggplot2::ggplot" "ggplot"          "ggplot2::gg"     "S7_object"  "gg"
```

### simple B subclass

```r
B <- new_class("B", class_ggplot, 
  properties=list(
    isB = new_property(getter = function(self) inherits(self, "B")),
    bprop = class_integer
  )
)
B(gg)@isB
# TRUE
B(gg)@bprop
# integer(0)
``` 

### simple C subclass

```r
C <- new_class("C", class_ggplot, 
  properties=list(
    isC = new_property(getter = function(self) inherits(self, "C")),
    cprop = class_logical
  )
)
C(B(gg))@isC
# [1] TRUE
C(B(gg)) |> class()
# [1] "C"               "ggplot2::ggplot" "ggplot2::gg"     "S7_object"
```

the `isB` prop doesn't exist

```r
C(B(gg))@isB
# Error: Can't find property <C>@isB
```

even though `B` is constructed first and would get the integer vector, that attribute is stripped

```r
attr(C(B(gg)), "bprop")
# NULL
``` 

Is the expected form for developers to eagerly transform classes with `S7::convert`?
What if during dispatch we just want to yield to the next logical class with `NextMethod()`? 
Even if we manually manipulate the class field, `C(B(gg))` will not have the class `B` within the parent chain.

title: Online inline class constructors if the package is the same
description:
Then we could remove the third current use case of `new_external_class()`:

> To use a class from another package as the parent of your own class. The parent's properties are captured when your class is defined, but its constructor is called at run time, so your subclass always builds on the installed version of the parent package.

title: Evolution vignette
description:
Need a vignette that systematically works through ways that classes and generics might change:

* Generic adds an argument
* Generic removes an argument
* Generic changes name
* Generic changes package
* Class adds a property (incl. potential to clash with subclasses)
* Class removes a property (incl. deprecation with active property)

This will be useful for future users, and will force us to ensure that we've fully thought through the key cases.

title: scalar properties
description:
Many times I would like to use a `class_string()` or `class_float()` which would be a character and double scalar respectively. I think this is a very common use case. 

Right now, we can use the rlang standalone type checks for making custom validators, but it would be exceptionally nice if these basic and common use cases were made available in S7. 

If this is something that the maintainers of S7 would support, I would be happy to make a PR.

Related-ish issue: https://github.com/RConsortium/S7/issues/412


Edit 2026-10-02: I've build [{s7x}](http://s7x.josiah.rs/) to fill this gap in the meantime.

title: S7 methods defined for S7 classes cannot be traced
description:
For example:

```R
library(S7)

type <- new_generic("type", "x")
data <- new_class("data")
method(type, data) <- function(x) {
  typeof(x)
}

object <- data()
type(object)
```

We'd like to be able to set a breakpoint inside the body of the defined function using `trace()`. I think we'd do this with something like:

```R
trace(data, where = type@methods)
```

but this fails with

```R
> trace("data", where = type@methods)
c("Constructing traceable class \"S7_methodWithTrace\"", "Constructing traceable class \"functionWithTrace\"", "Constructing traceable class \"S7_objectWithTrace\"")
c("Environment of class \"S7_method\" is locked; using global environment for new class", "Environment of class \"function\" is locked; using global environment for new class", "Environment of class \"S7_object\" is locked; using global environment for new class")
Error in !is.null(prototype) && is.na(match(name, .BasicClasses)) :
  'length = 3' in coercion to 'logical(1)'

title: Should `parent.frame()` in S7 methods match S3?
description:
Spun out from #592.

`parent.frame()` inside an S7 method currently differs from S3:

``` r
library(S7)

foo <- new_generic("foo", "x")
method(foo, class_any) <- function(x) parent.frame()

bar <- function(x) UseMethod("bar")
bar.default <- function(x) parent.frame()

foo(1)
#> <environment: 0x117954580>
bar(1)
#> <environment: R_GlobalEnv>
```


It would be nice if `parent.frame()` in an S7 method matched S3 here.

title: Default `print()` and `str()` trigger deprecated property warnings
description:
I came across this while working on https://github.com/tidyverse/ellmer/pull/1107/ and trying to deprecate a property of an S7 class.  

The default `print()`/`str()` for S7 objects call every property getter, so a deprecated property warns every time the object is printed.  The workaround is a custom `print()` method that filters those properties out, which is what the ellmer PR does.

There's some related discussion in #451, and #734 looks to implement `deprecated_property()`, but the missing piece is whether, once properties can be formally marked as deprecated, `print()` should skip them?

title: Can't deprecate generics
description:
While working on the evolution vignette (#143), we (well mostly Claude 😆) verified that the two existing ways to retire a generic's name each cover only half the problem:

* **Plain alias** (`gen1 <- gen2`, both exported): downstream method registrations keep working and both names dispatch (lab scenario `gen-rename-alias`), but callers get no deprecation signal.
* **Wrapper function** (`gen1 <- function(x, ...) { .Deprecated("gen2"); gen2(x, ...) }`): callers are warned, but a wrapper is not a generic, so every downstream `method(gen1, ...) <- ` errors and those packages can't even be installed.

Instead I think we should provide a first-class function to help do this:
```r
# pkgA, version 2
gen2 := new_generic("x")
gen1 := deprecated_generic(gen2)  # exported under the old name
```

The returned object is a closure with class `S7_deprecated_generic` that:

1. **On call**: signals a classed deprecation warning (probably once per session) and delegates to `gen2()` with all arguments.
2. **On registration**: `as_generic()` (and `as_external_generic()`) unwrap it, so `method(gen1, MyClass) <- f` registers on the shared `gen2`.
3. **On print/introspection**: identifies itself as deprecated and names the replacement.

Bonus properties:

* Mitigates #729 for renames: a stale downstream package's deferred registration looks up the old name, finds the deprecated-generic object, and unwraps it — instead of `library()` failing.
* Also the right endpoint for a generic *moved* to another package (`vignette("evolution")`'s move recipe): NAMESPACE re-export while alive, `deprecated_generic(pkgAcore::gen)` when retiring the old home.

Related: #727 is the class-side counterpart (renaming a class through an alias); #726 (graceful re-sourcing) is about the same check-vs-continue tension at method registration time.

I think the default should use `.Deprecated()` and but provide a callback so you can use lifecycle style if you want. Also needs to work with no existing generic to declare it's deprecated with no replacement.

title: Can't rename classes
description:
While verifying scenarios for the evolution vignette (#143): renaming a class breaks downstream packages *even when the old name is kept as an exported alias* (`Foo <- Bar`), if they refer to the class with `new_external_class("pkgA", "Foo")`:

```
Error: Package 'pkgA' must export `Foo` as the S7 class <pkgA::Foo>.
```

`resolve_external_class_req()` requires `identical(obj@name, name) && identical(obj@package, package)`, which an alias to the renamed class can't satisfy.

I suggest we drop this check.

title: Documenting S7 methods raises code/documentation mismatch warnings
description:
_Originally posted in https://github.com/r-lib/roxygen2/issues/1872_

Documenting S7 methods with additional non-generic arguments triggers CRAN check warnings since the methods themselves are invisible to the checks. I don't see an elegant fix for this without R changes that make the CRAN checks aware of S7 method arguments. An inelegant solution could be to separately document the S7 method usage and arguments in an Rd section (e.g. Methods) which is outside the attention of CRAN checks.

MRE:

```r
#' Size of an object
#'
#' @description
#' `size()` determines the size of an object.
#'
#' # Methods
#' `size()` is an S7 generic with methods available for the following
#' classes:
#'
#' `r doclisting::methods_list("size")`
#'
#' @param x An object.
#' @param ... Not used.
#' @returns A single number.
#' 
#' @export
size <- S7::new_generic("size", "x")

#' @rdname size
#' @param na.rm If TRUE, missing values are not included in the calculation of the size of an object.
S7::method(size, S7::class_any) <- function(x, ..., na.rm = FALSE) {
  if (na.rm) x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  length(x)
}
```

Produces the CRAN check warning:

```
❯ checking for code/documentation mismatches ... WARNING
  Codoc mismatches from Rd file 'size.Rd':
  size
    Code: function(x, ...)
    Docs: function(x, ..., na.rm = FALSE)
    Argument names in docs not in code:
      na.rm
```

---

The `tools::codoc()` function that detects these problems has special handling for finding S3 and S4 methods, and likely also needs special handling of S7 methods to allow them to be documented.

title: dump(<S7_object>)?
description:
I'm late to the party, and sorry if I missed a discussion on this, but is there a way to `dump()` an S7 object?  Attempting to do so gives:

```r
> x <- S7::S7_object()
> dump("x", file = stdout())
x <-
<object>
Warning message:
In dump("x", file = stdout()) : deparse may be incomplete
```

which is not valid R code.


Ultimately, I want to create a minimal, valid `S7_object` object _without_ using the 'S7' package. I want this in order to write a teeny 'codetools'-related unit test, without having to depend on the 'S7' package. Thus far, I know I can save an `S7_object` object to an RDS file, and obtain such a "creature" without having the 'S7' package installed, e.g.

> z
<object>
attr(,"class")
[1] "S7_object"
```

but it would be nice not to rely on a binary representation for my unit tests.

title: Think about how to store the class object
description:
Unfortunately `sys.function()` makes a deep copy of the class, meaning that we make a lot of unnecessary duplicates with both increases memory consumption and makes various `identical()` comparisons slower.

```R
library(S7)
library(lobstr)

compare_addresses <- function(...) {
  expressions <- as.list(substitute(list(...)))[-1]
  x <- list(...)
  addresses <- obj_addrs(x)

  data.frame(
    expression = vapply(expressions, deparse1, character(1)),
    address = addresses,
    same_as_first = addresses == addresses[[1]],
    row.names = NULL
  )
}

# Constructing instances ---------------------------------------------------

Foo := new_class(properties = list(x = class_double), package = NULL)
x <- Foo(x = 1)
y <- Foo(x = 2)

# On main, each instance contains a duplicate of Foo.
compare_addresses(
  Foo,
  S7_class(x),
  S7_class(y)
)

# Serializing a class ------------------------------------------------------

class_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(Foo, class_path)
Foo_rds <- readRDS(class_path)
x_rds <- Foo_rds(x = 1)
y_rds <- Foo_rds(x = 2)

compare_addresses(
  Foo_rds,
  S7_class(x_rds),
  S7_class(y_rds)
)

# The restored generator has a new address, as expected.
compare_addresses(Foo, Foo_rds)

# Serializing instances ---------------------------------------------------

instances_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(list(x, y), instances_path)
xy_rds <- readRDS(instances_path)

# Restored instances contain separate copies of the class.
# R's serializer preserves sharing for environments, but not closures.
compare_addresses(
  S7_class(xy_rds[[1]]),
  S7_class(xy_rds[[2]])
)

# Installing and loading a package ----------------------------------------

pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "s7address")
dir.create(file.path(pkg, "R"), recursive = TRUE)

writeLines(
  c(
    "Package: s7address",
    "Version: 0.0.0.9000",
    "Title: S7 Address Reprex",
    "Description: A temporary package used to inspect S7 class addresses.",
    "License: MIT",
    paste0(
      "Authors@R: person(\"A\", \"Person\", email = \"a@example.com\", ",
      "role = c(\"aut\", \"cre\"))"
    ),
    "Imports: S7"
  ),
  file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION")
)
writeLines(
  c(
    "export(Foo)",
    "importFrom(S7,\":=\")",
    "importFrom(S7,class_double)",
    "importFrom(S7,new_class)"
  ),
  file.path(pkg, "NAMESPACE")
)
writeLines(
  "Foo := new_class(properties = list(x = class_double))",
  file.path(pkg, "R", "classes.R")
)

lib <- file.path(tempdir(), "s7address-lib")
dir.create(lib)
install.packages(
  pkg,
  lib = lib,
  repos = NULL,
  type = "source",
  quiet = TRUE,
  INSTALL_opts = c("--no-byte-compile", "--no-test-load")
)

invisible(loadNamespace("s7address", lib.loc = lib))
pkg_Foo <- getExportedValue("s7address", "Foo")
pkg_x <- pkg_Foo(x = 1)
pkg_y <- pkg_Foo(x = 2)

compare_addresses(
  pkg_Foo,
  S7_class(pkg_x),
  S7_class(pkg_y)
)
```

title: Factor slots cannot contain missing values
description:
## Problem

In the dev version of `S7` the validator function of `class_factor` is now called at object construction time so that factor slots will crash if there are `NA`.  

## Previous Behavior

In previous versions you could do the following:

```r
value <- c(NA, 1)
TestObj <- S7::new_class(
    "TestObj",
    properties = list(val = S7::class_factor)
)
TestObj(val = value)
#> <TestObj>
#>  @ val: Factor w/ 1 level "x": NA 1
```

## New Behavior

But now what you get is this 

```r
TestObj <- S7::new_class(
    "TestObj",
    properties = list(val = S7::class_factor)
)
TestObj(val = value)
#> Error in `if (rng[1] < 0L) ...`:
#> ! missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```

## Possible Fix

The reason why this happens is because `validate_factor()` has the line `rng <- range(0L, unclass(self))` which produces `c(NA, NA)`. Adding `na.rm = TRUE` to the `range()` call would fix that:

```r
class_factor <- S7::class_factor
class_factor$validator <- function(self) {
    c(
        if (typeof(self) != "integer") "Underlying data must be an <integer>",
        if (!is.character(attr(self, "levels", TRUE))) {
            "attr(, 'levels') must be a <character>"
        },
        {
            rng <- range(0L, unclass(self), na.rm = TRUE) # add na.rm here
            NULL
        },
        if (rng[1] < 0L) "Underlying data must be all positive",
        if (rng[2] > length(attr(self, "levels", TRUE))) {
            "Not enough 'levels' for underlying data"
        }
    )
}
TestObj <- S7::new_class(
    "TestObj",
    properties = list(val = class_factor)
)
TestObj(val = value)
#> <TestObj>
#>  @ val: Factor w/ 1 level "x": NA 1
```

title: Can't change default arguments
description:
Found while verifying scenarios for the evolution vignette (#143).

When pkgA changes the default value of a non-dispatch argument of a generic, every downstream method that spells out the old default triggers the default-mismatch warning from `check_method()`:

```
Warning: In gen(<pkgB::BClass>), default value of `drop` is not the same as the generic
- Generic: TRUE
- Method:  FALSE
```

This warning fires when pkgB is installed (an `R CMD check` WARNING via "significant warnings") and again on every load (a check NOTE). Unlike adding an argument — where a method can include the new argument ahead of time and is silently accepted by both old and new generic — there is **no version of the method that is warning-free under both versions of pkgA**: whichever default it picks disagrees with one of them. So pkgA can't change a default without making every downstream package's checks noisy for the duration of the transition, no matter how cooperative the downstream authors are.

Maybe we only fire this when running R CMD check for pkgB or under pkgload? (i.e. `_R_CHECK_PACKAGE_NAME_`)

Related: because dispatch passes the *method's* formals, the method's default is what callers actually get, so these mismatches are genuine behavioral drift — whatever mechanism we pick should preserve that signal.

title: Allow a package to be re-sourced while methods are out of sync with a changed generic
description:
Split out from the discussion in #143:

> One last note: when you change a `generic()` it's nice to be able to still successfully source the whole package so that you can fix methods one-by-one, rather than having to update them all before your package re-loads successfully.

Today, changing a generic's interface makes `method<-` error at registration time via `check_method()`, so `devtools::load_all()` (and installation) fails until *every* method has been updated. The errors come from:

* A generic without `...`: method formals must match the generic's formals exactly.
* The method's leading arguments must match the generic's dispatch args, in order.
* Dispatch args must not have default values.

(Argument additions and default-value changes are already only warnings.)

Whatever the design, `R CMD check` should still surface the inconsistency loudly; the goal is only to keep the package sourceable mid-refactor.

title: Constructor performance
description:
While chatting at useR in Warsaw, @bnaras mentioned that the performance of the S7 constructor could be improved for performance-sensitive applications such as CVXR. This also matches our experience in r-xla/anvl.

It would be good for us to optimize the generated constructor and/or `new_object()`. Some big performance gains seem achievable with a little caching. @bnaras was kind enough to share a script (generated with AI assistance) demonstrating this:


```r
## Self-contained reproducible example:
## The `paste` overhead in S7's object constructor, and how CVXR's
## `.fast_new` sidesteps it.
##
## THE PROBLEM
## -----------
## Every `new_object()` call rebuilds the class-dispatch vector via S7's
## internal `class_dispatch()`, which walks the parent chain and calls
##     S7_class_name(x)  ==  paste(c(x@package, x@name), collapse = "::")
## once per level.  For a class N levels deep that is N `paste()` calls on
## EVERY construction -- yet the resulting vector
##     c("pkg::Var", "pkg::Leaf", "pkg::Expr", ..., "S7_object")
## is a CONSTANT of the class.  CVXR builds it once and caches it.
##
## Writeup: notes/s7_paste_overhead.md .  Canonical `.fast_new`:
## CVXR/rsrc_tree/zzz_R_specific/utility.R (ADR D_PERF.1).
##
## Run:  Rscript scripts/s7_paste_overhead.R

stopifnot(requireNamespace("S7", quietly = TRUE),
          requireNamespace("bench", quietly = TRUE))
library(S7)

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 1. A 5-level hierarchy, mimicking CVXR's Expression -> Leaf -> Variable
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Expr  <- new_class("Expr",  package = "demo",
                   properties = list(id = class_integer))
Node  <- new_class("Node",  parent = Expr,  package = "demo")
Atom  <- new_class("Atom",  parent = Node,  package = "demo")
Leaf  <- new_class("Leaf",  parent = Atom,  package = "demo")
Var   <- new_class("Var",   parent = Leaf,  package = "demo",
                   properties = list(nm = class_character),
                   ## a normal S7 constructor: the hot path we are measuring
                   constructor = function(id, nm) {
                     new_object(S7_object(), id = id, nm = nm)
                   })

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 2. CVXR-style .fast_new: cache the dispatch vector once per class,
##    attach attributes directly, skip validation.  Public S7 API only.
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
.fast_new <- local({
  cache <- new.env(hash = TRUE, parent = emptyenv())
  build_dispatch <- function(cls) {
    out <- character(0L); cur <- cls
    while (inherits(cur, "S7_class") && !identical(cur, S7::S7_object)) {
      out <- c(out, paste0(cur@package, "::", cur@name))   # paste PAID ONCE
      cur <- cur@parent
    }
    c(out, "S7_object")
  }
  function(.class, .parent, ...) {
    cn <- .class@name
    cd <- get0(cn, envir = cache, ifnotfound = NULL)
    if (is.null(cd)) { cd <- build_dispatch(.class); assign(cn, cd, cache) }
    obj <- .parent
    attributes(obj) <- c(list(class = cd, S7_class = .class), list(...))
    obj
  }
})

Var_fast <- function(id, nm) {
  if (FALSE) new_object(S7_object())          # S7 static-check guard
  .fast_new(Var, S7_object(), id = id, nm = nm)
}

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 3. Correctness: the two paths produce identical objects
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
a <- Var(1L, "x")
b <- Var_fast(1L, "x")
stopifnot(identical(class(a), class(b)),
          identical(a@id, b@id), identical(a@nm, b@nm),
          S7_inherits(b, Expr), S7_inherits(b, Leaf))
cat("class vector:", paste(class(a), collapse = " < "), "\n\n")

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 4. Where the time goes: profile 2e5 normal constructions
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
pf <- tempfile(fileext = ".out")
Rprof(pf, interval = 0.002)
for (i in 1:200000L) Var(i, "x")
Rprof(NULL)
cat("---- Rprof: self-time hot spots in the normal constructor ----\n")
print(head(summaryRprof(pf)$by.self, 12))

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 5. Benchmark: normal vs fast (report GC-free `min` and mem_alloc first)
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
cat("\n---- bench::mark (single construction) ----\n")
bm <- bench::mark(
  normal = Var(1L, "x"),
  fast   = Var_fast(1L, "x"),
  check = FALSE, min_iterations = 5000
)
print(bm[, c("expression", "min", "median", "mem_alloc", "n_gc")])
cat(sprintf("\nspeedup (median normal / median fast): %.1fx\n",
            as.numeric(bm$median[1]) / as.numeric(bm$median[2])))
```

This produces the following output with the current CRAN release of S7:

---- Rprof: self-time hot spots in the normal constructor ----

title: Can't move generics to another package
description:
Found while verifying the evolution vignette scenarios (#143), in the `gen-move-package` and `gen-rename` scenarios of `tools/evolution/`.

When pkgB has a deferred method registration whose generic no longer exists as a *direct* binding in the recorded package, loading pkgB fails hard:

```
Error: package or namespace load failed for 'evoB':
 .onLoad failed in loadNamespace() for 'evoB', details:
  call: get(generic$name, envir = ns, inherits = FALSE)
  error: object 'gen' not found
```

Two problems in `resolve_generic_opt()`:

1. **It errors instead of returning `NULL`.** `resolve_generic()` is written to warn `"[S7] Failed to find generic %s() in package %s"` when resolution fails, but `resolve_generic_opt()` uses `get()` rather than `get0()`, so a missing generic throws from inside the load hook and takes down `library(pkgB)` entirely. An installed pkgB should degrade to a warning when pkgA renames a generic, not become unloadable.

2. **It can't see re-exports.** `get(..., envir = ns, inherits = FALSE)` misses bindings that pkgA re-exports from another package (they live in the imports environment, not the namespace proper). So when pkgA moves a generic to pkgAcore and re-exports it every *already-installed* downstream package fails to load. Resolving via `getExportedValue()` (falling back to the namespace itself for own, unexported generics) would make the move seamless for stale installs too.

title: Parent class constructor defaults are not safely scoped in child constructors
description:
The default constructor's inheritance of parent constructor formals seems unsafe, since the evaluation environment might change. I encountered this when developing an S7 class in a package with a custom constructor, and then extending this class in a different package with the default constructor.

Perhaps passing parent properties to the parent constructor via `...` is a safer alternative? This would also fix #467 and #585.

Explanatory MRE:

``` r
library(S7)
```

The built-in constructor evaluates default arguments.

``` r
e <- new.env()
local({
  default <- 1L
  parent <- new_class(
    "parent",
    properties = list(
      x = new_property(class_integer, default = default)
    )
  )
}, envir = e)

# evaluated property defaults are used in formals
formals(e$parent)
#> $x
#> [1] 1
e$parent()
#> <parent>
#>  @ x: int 1
```

Suppose we prefer the constructor's formals to maintain the symbol defaults

```r
# Custom constructor for unevaluated defaults
local({
  default <- 1L
  parent <- new_class(
    "parent",
    properties = list(
      x = new_property(class_integer, default = default)
    ),
    constructor = function(x = default) {
      new_object(S7::S7_object(), x = x)
    }
  )
}, envir = e)

# Constructor with symbol property defaults used in formals
formals(e$parent)
#> $x
#> default
e$parent()
#> <parent>
#>  @ x: int 1
```

This works, the symbols are found from the correct environment when needed.

Then we inherit this class as a parent from a class in a different environment.

```r
child <- new_class(
  "child", 
  e$parent,
  properties = list(
    y = new_property(class_integer, default = 0L)
  )
)

# Parent constructor formals are copied to child constructor
# But the environment is now different, so the symbols cannot be found
formals(child)
#> $x
#> default
#> 
#> $y
#> [1] 0
child()
#> Error in `child()`:
#> ! object 'default' not found
```

The parent constructor's formals are merged with the child constructor's formals, and evaluated in the child constructor's environment -- so the symbol cannot be found.

If we instead pass through parent properties to the parent constructor via `...`, the appropriate arguments are evaluated in the appropriate environment.

```r

# Alternatively, passing ... to parent methods evaluates formals in the
# appropriate context/environment.
child <- new_class(
  "child", 
  e$parent,
  properties = list(
    y = new_property(class_integer, default = 0L)
  ),
  constructor = function(..., y = 0L) {
    new_object(e$parent(...), y = y)
  }
)
formals(child)
#> $...
#> 
#> 
#> $y
#> [1] 0
child()
#> <child>
#>  @ x: int 1
#>  @ y: int 0
```

<sup>Created on 2026-05-06 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

title: Extending a class from another package
description:
Currently if you extend a class from another package, the parent class will be captured at build-time. So if that package is later updated, and your package is not re-built, it's possible for two inconsistent versions of a class to exist. (The methods will be fine since they're already registered dynamically if needed, but the properties and validator might not).

We might be able to fix this and #250 at the same time by creating something like `new_external_class()` which contains just enough information to perform minimal static checks with the actual invocation always happening at run time. This will require some careful thought and analysis.

title: Dynamic properties are not checked for consistency with parent
description:
```R
foo := new_class(properties = list(x = class_integer))
foo2 := new_class(
  parent = foo,
  properties = list(
    x = new_property(
      class_character,
      getter = function(self) self@x,
      setter = function(self, value) {
        self@x <- value
        self
      }
    )
  )
)
```

This seems like a violation of #352, but was deliberately carved out of #691: https://github.com/RConsortium/S7/pull/691/changes#diff-db883c7d4a79cfb06f9b46be422e9619820b841e80f70a2592cad16653adebe6R444-R448

title: Mixing S4 and S7 inheritance hierarchies
description:
It may be possible to have an S4 object inherit from S7_object. Some things that would need to happen:

- To enable an S4 class inheriting from an S7 class, `S4_register()` would need to pass a transient class to `S4Class=` on `setOldClass()` to establish the inherited slots on the S4 class.
- To enable S7 extending S4, we would need to remove the `stop()` and figure out things like how to construct the parent S4 instance, allow access to the S4 properties in `prop_set_()` and probably other things.
- To enable either direction, and support getters/setters on the S7 properties, `@()` would need to prioritize dispatch (instead of guarding against S4 objects). This would have a performance impact on S4 code that uses a lot of `@()`. We may have to sacrifice that feature for now.

title: Design of `super()` encourages tight coupling between implementation code and class hierarchy
description:
I'm expanding this issue from this comment since I think it is a separate issue: https://github.com/RConsortium/S7/issues/493#issuecomment-2480988877

Having used S7 to build out an API making extensive use of multiple dispatch, I'd like to offer some thoughts and a suggestion for a minor change in the API that I think would make it easier to use. I think this suggested change is in keeping with the explicitness that motivated `super()` in the first place, but which improves maintainability of code both within and (importantly) across packages.

### The problem: `super()` has two meanings in use and one is tightly coupled to the class hierarchy

I think `super()` is misnamed, and its suggested method of use creates a tight coupling between implementation code and the class hierarchy.

Consider a class hierarchy with base class `BaseClass`, child `Child`, and a binary operator `op`:

```r
BaseClass = new_class("BaseClass")
Child = new_class("Child", parent = BaseClass)

op = new_generic("op", c("x", "y"))

method(op, list(BaseClass, BaseClass)) = \(x, y) {
  # do stuff on BaseClass
}
```

If I had an implementation for `op` on `Child` with any other `BaseClass` (ignore commutativity --- in practice I would also have an implementation for `(BaseClass, Child)`), it might look something like:

```r
method(op, list(Child, BaseClass)) = \(x, y) {
  # do stuff on Child, then...
  op(super(x, BaseClass), super(y, BaseClass))
}
```

Semantically, within the context of this method implementation, the line `op(super(x, BaseClass), super(y, BaseClass))` has two different modes of dispatch:

1. `super(x, BaseClass)` for `x`, a `Child` (or subclass of `Child`): this is used to mean "dispatch one class up in the hierarchy" or "dispatch to the parent of `Child`".
2. `super(y, BaseClass)` for `y`, a `BaseClass` (or a subclass of `BaseClass`): this is used to mean "dispatch on the same class again" or "dispatch on `BaseClass`".

The second meaning works well, since as the implementor of this method I know that `BaseClass` is precisely the class I want to target for dispatch of `y`.

However, the first meaning couples the class hierarchy as it currently stands with this implementation of the method `op`. If the hierarchy of `Child` changes at some point in the future, as an implementor I must also update every method of `Child` relying on this hierarchy to dispatch to a parent class. For example, say we later add a class in between `BaseClass` and `Child`, changing the parent of `Child`:

```r
IntermediateClass = new_class("IntermediateClass", parent = BaseClass)
Child = new_class("Child", parent = IntermediateClass)
```

Now the definition of `op` should be:

```r
method(op, list(Child, BaseClass)) = \(x, y) {
  # do stuff on Child, then...
  op(super(x, IntermediateClass), super(y, BaseClass))
}
```

Besides creating maintenance issues within a single package, if `BaseClass` and `Child` are implemented in one package and `op` in another, now we have a tight coupling across package boundaries, creating even worse maintenance issues.

### Solution 1: encourage use of `@parent` with `super()` for use case 1

One solution would be to implement `op` as:

```r
method(op, list(Child, BaseClass)) = \(x, y) {
  # do stuff on Child, then...
  op(super(x, Child@parent), super(y, BaseClass))
}
```

This works, though not on S3 classes since `S7_S3_class` doesn't have `@parent`. This solution could be adopted just by updating some documentation and recommended use, and probably also by adding a unified interface for getting a class's parent (which would be helpful to have anyway).

However, to me this reveals another issue: `super()` is not well-named. The first operation (`super(x, Child@parent)`) is much closer to what I would normally think of as a `super()` operation (dispatch on the superclass), and it feels redundant to write both `super` and `@parent`; on the other hand, the second operation (`super(y, BaseClass)`) is more like "dispatch on exactly this class", so the use of the word `super` feels incorrect. This motivates my second suggestion.

### Solution 2: split `super()` into two operations

My suggestion is to split `super()` into two operations, each reflecting their appropriate use in context. Something like `dispatch_up()` or `dispatch_parent()` for the first operation, which would dispatch to the parent of the second argument, and something like `dispatch()` for what is currently called `super()`.

FWIW, I have been using helpers defining `dispatch_up()` and `dispatch()` in this way (also addressing dispatch on class unions as described in https://github.com/RConsortium/S7/issues/493#issuecomment-2481027340), and it has already saved me maintenance work when refactoring a class hierarchy. Had I not done so I would have had to refactor a few dozen methods for a single change in the class hierarchy, but using `dispatch_up()` I didn't have to touch those methods at all. The code also reads more clearly: I know precisely which of the two uses of `super` is intended by a call based on what function is used.

title: Generic unions
description:
While I was waiting on #353 and #365, I started playing with an alternative approach to group generics in a package I am working on. I think this approach may be simpler than the current proposal, and also offer several benefits.

The basic idea is to add a general mechanism by which people can define methods on sets of generics at once. This could be implemented within `method<-`, or using a separate function.

The simple (probably not robust) implementation I am currently using looks like this:

```r
#' Define methods on a group of generics
#'
#' Takes a list of generic functions and defines the same function for each,
#' allowing use of `.Generic` in the function body to refer to the actual generic.
#' @param generics a list of [symbol]s (such as returned by [expression()]),
#' each of which should correspond to a generic function, or the S4 definition
#' of a group generic, such as [`Compare`].
#' @param signature A method signature (see [`method<-`])
#' @param value A function implementing each `generic` for the given `signature`.
#' In each method, the variable `.Generic` in the method's environment will
#' refer to the generic function.
#' @noRd
`group_method<-` = \(generics, signature, value) {
  .generics = if (is(generics, "groupGenericFunction")) {
    lapply(getGroupMembers(generics), as.symbol)
  } else {
    generics
  }

  for (generic in .generics) {
    f = value
    environment(f) = new.env(parent = environment(value))
    environment(f)$.Generic = get(generic, mode = "function")
    eval(bquote(
      method(.(generic), signature) <<- f
    ))
  }
  invisible(generics)
}
```

Then you can use any existing S4 group generic as follows (say on a toy numeric class, "MyNum"):

```r
group_method(Compare, list(MyNum, MyNum)) = \(e1, e2) MyNum(value = .Generic(e1@value, e2@value))
```

Since this generates all the specific methods (instead of creating a parallel dispatch on group generics), I think it makes dispatch easier to understand and easier to extend when creating class hierarchies. 

It also avoids some of the ugliness common to S3 / S4 group generics code, like switch statements singling out one or two methods that operate differently. Instead, you would just define the specific methods you want to create as a separate group. e.g. if I just wanted to override inequalities, I might do:

```r
inequalities = expression(`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`)    # or probably new_group_generic(...) or something
group_method(inequalities, list(MyNum, MyNum)) = \(e1, e2) MyNum(value = .Generic(e1@value, e2@value))
```

This also avoids the need for a method to look up the actual generic function inside the implementation, and allows users to create their own groups of generics as needed.

title: Defining generic methods for suggested packages
How to create a nestable R7 class?
description:
Sometimes it's useful to be able to nest objects of the same type inside each other.  Is there a recommended way for doing this with R7?

##  Naive approach
It's good that this errors; if you ever tried to instantiate this you'd end up in an infinitely recursing loop.

``` r
nested <- new_class("nested",
  properties = list(child = nested)
)
#> Error in as_properties(properties): object 'nested' not found
```

<sup>Created on 2022-08-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

## `new_union()`
It would be nice if this worked, allowing you to specify at least one other type that can be a "base case". Preferably while still protecting you from infinite recursion by not permitting the nested class to be the default.

``` r
nested <- new_class("nested",
  properties = list( child = new_union(NULL, nested) )
)
#> Error in lapply(x, as_class): object 'nested' not found
```

<sup>Created on 2022-08-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

## Define it twice

This doesn't error and lets me nest objects, but `properties` holds on to the original class definition (`inner`'s child has no `name` or `child` properties, since the original definition of `nested` had no properties).  I don't know what problems that might cause (and it prevents the infinite recursion problem), but I don't like the feel of it.

``` r
nested <- new_class("nested")

nested <- new_class("nested",
  properties = list( 
    name = class_character,
    child = nested )
)

inner <- nested()
inner
#> <nested>
#>  @ name : chr(0) 
#>  @ child: <nested>

outer <- nested(name = "outer", child = inner)
outer
#> <nested>
#>  @ name : chr "outer"
#>  @ child: <nested>
#>  .. @ name : chr(0) 
#>  .. @ child: <nested>
```

<sup>Created on 2022-08-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

# Use a parent class

This seems to work and I haven't thougth of anything that would go wrong.  It's mildly annoying to have the extra parent class cluttering things up if I don't have any other reason for it to exist, but I can live with it :)

``` r
nested_parent <- new_class("nested_parent")

nested <- new_class("nested", parent = nested_parent,
  properties = list( 
    name = class_character,
    child = nested_parent )
)

inner <- nested()
inner
#> <nested>
#>  @ name : chr(0) 
#>  @ child: <nested_parent>

outer <- nested(name = "outer", child = inner)
outer
#> <nested>
#>  @ name : chr "outer"
#>  @ child: <nested>
#>  .. @ name : chr(0) 
#>  .. @ child: <nested_parent>
```

<sup>Created on 2022-08-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

So, 2 requests:
1. It'd be nice to have documentation on the recommended way to create nestable classes. Is using a parent class the way to go?
2. Any chance some behind-the-scenes wizardry could make something like the `new_union` syntax work?

title: [Feature Request] Interface for validation logic and names of `class_*` wrappers
description:
I keep working more and more with S7 and find it very useable in general. One thing I do keep stumbling on repeatedly is using many of the `class_*`  wrappers for type checks as part of my code. 

## Motivation

For example, I'm trying to create functions that allow users to have more type safety with dataframes. For example, imagine that I have another `class_*` wrapper around `class_data.frame` that allows me to validate column types. Let's call this function `S7_class_data_frame()`.

Then I could create a specific df type like so

```
class_typed_df <- S7_class_data_frame(
    x = S7::class_numeric,
    y = S7::class_character,
    z = S7::class_double
)
```

With this, I could use the internal `prop_validate()` function to test arbitrary data.frames:

```r
S7:::prop_validate(class_typed_df, data.frame(x = 1, y = "bla", z = 1.0))
# NULL

S7:::prop_validate(class_typed_df, data.frame(x = 1, y = 1))
# [1] " Column `y` has wrong type. Expected <character>. Got <numeric>."
# [2] " Column `z` has wrong type. Expected <double>. Got <NULL>." 
```

This is convenient because I don't necessarily want to wrap every data frame into another object to do the type checking. But currently I'm forced to use an internal function for this.

Or I could have my typed DF as part of an S7 object (possibly to bring along metadata that I don't bother mocking here):

```r
TestTypedDFClass <- S7::new_class(
    "TestTypedDFClass",
    properties = list(
        df = class_typed_df
    )
)

TestTypedDFClass(df = data.frame(x = 1, y = 'bla', z = 1.0))
# <TestTypedDFClass>
#  @ df:'data.frame':	1 obs. of  3 variables:
#  .. $ x: num 1
#  .. $ y: chr "bla"
#  .. $ z: num 1

TestTypedDFClass(df = data.frame(x = 1, y = 2))
# Error:
# ! <TestTypedDFClass> object properties are invalid:
# - @df Column `y` has wrong type. Expected <character>. Got <numeric>.
# - @df Column `z` has wrong type. Expected <double>. Got <NULL>.
```

Now this implementation relies on two things:

1. I can (in)validate arbitrary `class_*` wrappers
2. I can grab the name of types (to create the messages for the validator)

If we assume that a function `is_incorrect_type()` addresses 1 and another function `s7_class_name()` addresses 2, then an implementation of `S7_class_data_frame()` could look like this:

```r
S7_class_data_frame <- function(...) {
    S7::new_property(
        class = S7::class_data.frame,
        validator = function(value) {
            purrr::imap(
                list(...),
                \(expected_class, col_name) {
                    column_is_incorrect_type <- is_incorrect_type(
                        value[[col_name]],
                        expected_class
                    )
                    if (column_is_incorrect_type) {
                        got <- class(value[[col_name]])[[1]]
                        expected <- s7_class_name(expected_class)
                        glue::glue(
                            'Column `{col_name}` has wrong type. Expected <{expected}>. Got <{got}>.'
                        )
                    }
                }
            ) |>
                unlist()
        }
    )
}
```

I think that it would be nice if the S7 package exposes some interface that would make it easy to write such validators for custom types. Currently, I had to rely on internal S7 functions to make that work. That exposed me to inconsistencies I did not understand (probably skill issue on my behalf because I missunderstand some underlying design pattern) and forced me to write my own (probably) clunky wrappers around S7 internals. This feature request is about showcasing these inconsistencies so that maybe a nicer public interface could be added to S7.

## Validation

For some validations I used the internal function `S7:::class_validate()`. For primitives that works as expected:

```r
S7:::class_validate(S7::class_character, 123)
# [1] "Underlying data must be <character> not <double>"

S7:::class_validate(S7::class_character, "bla") |> is.null()
# [1] TRUE

S7:::class_validate(S7::class_character, 123) |> is.null()
# [1] FALSE
```

For `S7_union` types `class_validate()` seems to not behave as I'd expect:

```r
# Makes sense to me
S7:::class_validate(S7::class_numeric, 123)
# NULL

# Seems odd. I'd expect # [1] "Underlying data must be <numeric> not <character>"
S7:::class_validate(S7::class_numeric, "")
# NULL
```

I'm guessing I misunderstand how `class_numeric` is normally validated but it would be nice to have a public function that can do these validations. My current workaround is to create a function that keeps track of unions....

<details>
<summary>Helper function: get_list_subtypes</summary>

```r
get_list_subtypes <- function(s7_union) {
    if (identical(s7_union, S7::class_numeric)) {
        return(list(S7::class_integer, S7::class_double))
    }

    if (identical(s7_union, S7::class_atomic)) {
        return(
            list(
                S7::class_logical,
                S7::class_numeric,
                S7::class_complex,
                S7::class_character,
                S7::class_raw
            )
        )
    }

    if (identical(s7_union, S7::class_vector)) {
        return(
            list(
                S7::class_logical,
                S7::class_numeric,
                S7::class_complex,
                S7::class_character,
                S7::class_raw,
                S7::class_list,
                S7::class_expression
            )
        )
    }

    if (identical(s7_union, S7::class_language)) {
        return(
            list(
                S7::class_name,
                S7::class_call
            )
        )
    }

    cli::cli_abort("Unsupported S7 Union type")
}
```

</details>


... and then call that iteratively. Probably not good design but maybe some of the code is reusable for others reading this.

<details>
<summary>Function: is_incorrect_type</summary>

```r
#' Check if a Value Has an Incorrect Type
#'
#' Determines whether a given `value` does not conform to an expected S7 class
#' or property. Supports S7 properties, union classes, base classes, and regular
#' S7 classes.
#'
#' @param value The object to validate.
#' @param expected_class An S7 class or property definition that `value` is
#'   expected to conform to.
#'
#' @details
#' The function performs different validation strategies depending on the type
#' of `expected_class`:
#' \describe{
#'   \item{S7 properties (`S7_property`)}{Uses internal property validation via
#'   \code{S7:::prop_validate()} and returns \code{TRUE} if validation fails.}
#'   \item{S7 union classes (`S7_union`)}{Checks all subtypes and returns
#'   \code{TRUE} only if validation fails for every subtype.}
#'   \item{S7 base classes (`S7_S3_class`, `S7_base_class`, or `S7_any`)}{
#'   Uses internal S7 validation via \code{S7:::class_validate()} and returns
#'   \code{TRUE} if validation fails.}
#'   \item{Other classes}{Checks inheritance using \code{S7::S7_inherits()}.}
#' }
#'
#' @return Logical scalar. \code{TRUE} if `value` is not of the expected type,
#'   \code{FALSE} otherwise.
#'
#' @export
is_incorrect_type <- function(value, expected_class) {
    expected_class_type <- attributes(expected_class)$class

    is_s7_property <- any(expected_class_type == "S7_property")
    if (is_s7_property) {
        return(!is.null(S7:::prop_validate(expected_class, value)))
    }

    is_s7_union <- any(expected_class_type == "S7_union")
    if (is_s7_union) {
        list_subtypes <- get_list_subtypes(expected_class)
        all_subtype_validations_fail <- list_subtypes |>
            purrr::map(\(x) S7:::class_validate(x, value)) |>
            purrr::every(\(x) !is.null(x)) |>
            all()
        return(all_subtype_validations_fail)
    }

    is_base_class <- any(
        c("S7_S3_class", "S7_base_class", "S7_any") %in%
            expected_class_type
    )
    if (is_base_class) {
        validation_string <- S7:::class_validate(expected_class, value)
        return(!is.null(validation_string))
    }

    !S7::S7_inherits(value, expected_class)
}

is_incorrect_type(123, S7::class_numeric)
# [1] FALSE
is_incorrect_type("", S7::class_numeric)
# [1] TRUE
```


</details>


## Class names

Similarly, it could be helpful to have a way to access the type names of all the `class_*`  wrappers. By accident (not sure if that's documented) I found that `$class` can be used but for unions like `class_numeric` that yields unexpected (at least to me) behavior:

```r
# Expected
S7::class_double$class
# [1] "double"

# Would have expected "numeric" as a result
S7::class_numeric$class
# [[1]]
# <S7_base_class>: <integer>
# 
# [[2]]
# <S7_base_class>: <double>
```

And as for S7 objects, it might be beneficial to have a wrapper function that returns a class name. So when `x` is of type `MyObject`, then `S7_class_name()` returns `"MyObject"`. Essentially a wrapper around this (which I couldn't find in the documentation and then stumbled on this idea by accident):

```r
x >  
  S7::S7_class()  |>
  S7::prop('name')
```

A current (somewhat silly) workaround I'm using to handle all of these cases is documented in this function;

<details>
<summary>Function: Class names</summary>


```r
#' Get S7 Class or Property Name
#'
#' Returns a human-readable name for a given S7 class, property, or object.
#' Handles S7 properties, user-defined S7 classes (via instances), and
#' built-in/base S7 classes, including unions.
#'
#' @param cls An S7 class, property definition, or S7 object instance.
#'
#' @details
#' The function distinguishes between different types of S7 inputs:
#' \describe{
#'   \item{S7 properties (`S7_property`)}{Returns the property name via
#'   \code{cls$name}.}
#'   \item{Custom S7 classes or objects}{Attempts to retrieve the class name
#'   from the underlying S7 class definition using
#'   \code{S7::S7_class()} followed by \code{S7::prop("name")}.
#'   Returns \code{"<anonymous>"} if unavailable.}
#'   \item{Base or union classes (`S7_S3_class`, `S7_base_class`, `S7_union`)}{
#'   Matches the class against known S7 base class wrappers and returns a
#'   descriptive name (e.g., \code{"character"},
#'   \code{"numeric (union of integer and double)"}).}
#' }
#'
#' @return A character vector of length one containing the class or property name.
#'
#' @export
s7_class_name <- function(cls) {
    is_s7_property <- any(class(cls) == "S7_property")
    if (is_s7_property) {
        return(cls$name)
    }

    is_base_class <- any(
        c("S7_S3_class", "S7_base_class", "S7_union") %in% attributes(cls)
    )
    if (!is_base_class) {
        fallback <- tryCatch(
            cls |>
                S7::S7_class() |>
                S7::prop('name'),
            error = \(e) NULL
        )
        return(fallback %||% "<anonymous>")
    }

    l <- list(
        "factor" = S7::class_factor,
        "Date" = S7::class_Date,
        "POSIXct" = S7::class_POSIXct,
        "POSIXlt" = S7::class_POSIXlt,
        "POSIXt" = S7::class_POSIXt,
        "data.frame" = S7::class_data.frame,
        "formula" = S7::class_formula,
        "logical" = S7::class_logical,
        "integer" = S7::class_integer,
        "double" = S7::class_double,
        "complex" = S7::class_complex,
        "character" = S7::class_character,
        "raw" = S7::class_raw,
        "list" = S7::class_list,
        "expression" = S7::class_expression,
        "name" = S7::class_name,
        "call" = S7::class_call,
        "function" = S7::class_function,
        "environment" = S7::class_environment,
        "numeric (union of integer and double)" = S7::class_numeric,
        "atomic (union of logical, numeric, complex, character, and raw)" = S7::class_atomic,
        "vector (union of atomic, list, and expression)" = S7::class_vector,
        "language (name and call)" = S7::class_language
    )

    purrr::keep(l, \(s7_class_wrapper) identical(cls, s7_class_wrapper)) |>
        names()
}
```


</details>

title: S7 class / object identity across lazy loading when using local enclosures
description:
Consider two packages `A` and `B`:

```r
# In package A
class_A <- local({
  threshold <- 10L
  new_class("class_A", ..., validator = function(self) ...)
})

# In package B
my_class_A <- class_A
make_both <- function(x) list(
  my = my_class_A(x = x),
  direct = class_A(x = x)
)

# In .GlobalEnv
both <- B::make_both("foo")
identity(both$my, both$direct) # FALSE
```

The validator of `class_A` has a local enclosure. If package B assigns the class object into its namespace, R will obviously not be able to preserve object identity across package load due to the local enclosure (identity can only be preserved when the enclosure is a namespace).

I'm not sure if there's a better solution than just warning in the docs not to do any class object renaming within a client namespace.

title: Child class property setters that mask parent class properties are unused at construction
description:
Given a set of child-parent classes, where the child masks a parent property and adds a custom setter such as

```r
parent <- new_class(
  "parent",
  properties = list(
    "x" = class_integer,
    "y" = class_character,
    "z" = class_any
  )
)

child <- new_class(
  "child",
  parent = parent,
  properties = list(
    "z" = new_property(
      class_double,
      setter = function(self, value) {
        stop("hey! don't set that!")
        self
      }
    )
  )
)
```

Calling the child constructor does not ever hit the child property setter.

```r
child(z = 1)
```
```
<child>
 @ x: int(0)
 @ y: chr(0)
 @ z: num 1
```

I would expect that calling `child(z = 1)` would use the child property setter and throw the error, but it seems that the parent constructor is used then the value is type checked against the child property class without ever using the child setter.

title: Default value introduced in subclass does not propagate to constructor
description: This [line](https://github.com/RConsortium/S7/blob/b5cf389d7c6dc676c2d938e2feac6d7ec04d0c50/R/constructor.R#L64) drops the parent properties from the constructor by name; however, I think it's valid for subclasses to add/change the default for a parent property. Since we're dropping the subclass properties, the changed default does not make it to the constructor. Self args should probably be kept (and override the parent) if they have a different default.

title: Unregister methods on unload
description: `methods_register()` also needs add a hook on package unload to remove all methods, and reset any unused hooks.

title: Consider example of multiple dispatch with `intersect(x, y)`
description:
Could be added to this section
https://rconsortium.github.io/S7/articles/generics-methods.html#multiple-dispatch

See also this thread
https://fosstodon.org/@jonocarroll/112913640978442903

`intersect(x, y)` is not a generic function in base R. We introduced the {generics} R package to turn it into a generic, so we could write methods on them in classes throughout the tidyverse - but the generic only dispatches on `x` and then it is up to the method to ensure that `y` is the right class.

It might be interesting to implement `intersect(x, y)` using multiple dispatch as a motivating example for that feature. I imagine that 99.99% of the time, you will end up only implementing a method for the case where `x` and `y` are the same type, i.e. for when they are both `Date`. But being able to express this in the type system rather than having the method confirm that `y` is the right type seems nice.

title: Should property defaults be required to be `quote()`d?
Boost `local_s4_class()`
Use `test_that()` consistently
Extending a parent class with inconsistent properties
description:
Currently it's possible to define a class whose properties are inconsistent with its parent:

``` r
library(S7)

foo1 <- new_class("foo1", properties = list(x = class_integer))
foo2 <- new_class("foo2", parent = foo1, properties = list(x = class_character))
```

This doesn't error when you create the class, but it's not possible to construct it because there's no value that will satisfy the validator of both `foo1` and `foo2`:

``` r
foo2(x = 1L)
#> Error: <foo2> object properties are invalid:
#> - @x must be <character>, not <integer>
foo2(x = "x")
#> Error: <foo1> object properties are invalid:
#> - @x must be <integer>, not <character>
```

Should we make this a define-time error? In principle, I think it's ok for a child class to make a property more restrictive than the parent class, but there's no way to test for test for this in general (since the restriction may occur at the validator level).

title: Multiple constructors? / Separation of S7 classes and constructors
description:
Thank you for pushing this wonderful project forward. It looks very promising.

I've read the documentation, but in the current implementation, S7 class instances can only exist via the single constructor?
I have tried to imagine creating a wrapper object for an external pointer (specifically something like Series in [the polars package](https://github.com/pola-rs/r-polars)) in S7.

For example, the constructor must take a name (string) and values (R vector) and construct an external pointer stored in `_s`. (Note: Because it mimics Python's polars package)
The name can be changed later so it becomes a property.

```r
s_foo <- Series(name = "foo", values = 1)

s_foo@name
#> foo
s_foo@`_s`
#> <external pointer>

# The name can be changed
s_foo@name <- "bar"
s_foo@name
#> bar

# The pointer should be frozen
s_foo@`_s` <- other_pointer
#> Error
```

But apart from this, it also requires an (internal-only) function to create objects by directly setting an external pointer.
Is it possible to create such a thing?
Ideally, it would be called a class method or an associated function (related to #202, #436), but it does not have to be.

```py
# In Python Polars, there are two class methods to construct Series
Series._from_pyseries() # From Rust / Rust Polars' Series
Series._import_from_c() # From C / Apache Arrow C interface
```

```r
# In R, something like these:
Series@.from_rseries()
Series@.import_from_c()

# These internal functions are also fine
series_from_rseries()
series_import_from_c()
```

I want to export the S7 object itself (`Series`) for use in the `convert` function, etc., but do not want to export the constructor for manipulating the external pointer.
Therefore, I do not want the default constructor to be one that takes an external pointer.

```r
# The S7 object should be exported
Series
# Because it will be used with the `convert` function
convert(1, Series)
convert(a_nanoarrow_array_stream, Series)

# But I don't want to expose the constructor that builds the Series from an external pointer something like this
Series(.data = rust_series)
```

title: Missing (equivalent of) S3 / S4   `methods(class = .)`  to get all generics for which there are <class>-methods

title: Constructors: Using `rlang::inject` with `new_object()`
description:
Is there a way to use `rlang::inject` (or something similar) with `new_object`? It currently throws an error that `new_object()` must be called from within a constructor. Here's a reprex:

``` r
library(S7)
library(rlang)
library(purrr)
library(palmerpenguins)

# My real use case involves JSON data, so we'll transform into a list. 
my_penguin <- as.list(penguins[1,])

penguin <- new_class(
  "penguin",
  properties = list(
    species = class_factor,
    island = class_factor,
    bill_length_mm = class_double,
    bill_depth_mm = class_double,
    flipper_length_mm = class_integer,
    body_mass_g = class_integer,
    sex = class_factor,
    year = class_integer
  ),
  constructor = function(x) {
    # The `penguins` data frame contains all the possible properties for `penguin` objects.
    # For my real use case, these properties would be read from a JSON Schema file.
    penguins_properties <- set_names(colnames(penguins))
    # I want to pluck the property values for `my_penguin` as a named list that can be used
    # to construct the object.
    out <- map(penguins_properties, function(y) pluck(x, y))
    # This throws an error.
    inject(new_object(S7_object(), !!!out))
  }
)

penguin(my_penguin)
#> Error in new_object(S7_object(), species = structure(1L, levels = c("Adelie", : `new_object()` must be called from within a constructor
```

title: Feature request: pass `name` to property setter
description:
I've found it useful to declare properties outside a class definition and recycle the property definition for various classes or for similar properties within one class.
The issue I'm running in to is that property setters don't have access to the name of the property that is being set.
In the example below, I cannot recycle the colour property for `fill`, because the setter function hardcodes the name.

``` r
library(S7)

property_colour <- new_property(
  class = class_character,
  setter = function(self, value) {
   # Must I hardcode the property name?
    prop(self, "colour") <- as.character(value)
    self
  }
)

rectangle <- new_class(
  "rectangle",
  properties = list(
    colour = property_colour, 
    fill = property_colour
  )
)

x <- rectangle("red", "blue")
#> Error: <rectangle> object properties are invalid:
#> - @fill must be <character>, not <NULL>
```

<sup>Created on 2025-07-23 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

My current solution to this problem is to make a property factory like so:

``` r
library(S7)

property_colour <- function(name) {
  force(name)
  new_property(
    class = class_character,
    setter = function(self, value) {
      prop(self, name) <- as.character(value)
      self
    }
  )
}

rectangle <- new_class(
  "rectangle",
  properties = list(
    colour = property_colour("colour"), 
    fill = property_colour("fill")
  )
)

x <- rectangle("red", "blue")
```

<sup>Created on 2025-07-23 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

But this solution is a bit unwieldy because I still have to declare the `"colour"` and `"fill"` names twice: once in the list names and once as argument to `property_colour()`. If we could somehow automatically access the property name that is being set from the context of the setter function, this would be a much smoother experience.
